title: How My Goals Above Replacement (GAR) Stat Works
subtitle: A single number, measured in goals, for every skater and goalie season in NHL history, that adds up to team-wide performance.

How NHL GAR Works

GAR stands for Goals Above Replacement. The basic question is familiar enough: How many goals was a player worth compared with what his team could have gotten from a replacement-level alternative?

The harder part is answering that question consistently for everybody from a 1918 rover to a 2026 shutdown defenseman.

The current version of GAR covers 57,206 player-team-seasons, spanning 8,778 players and all 108 seasons in NHL history.

Most public player-value metrics are built from the bottom up. They assign value to individual events, add everything together and accept whatever leaguewide total comes out the other end. Like its cousin, Approximate Value in football, GAR starts in the opposite direction. First, it determines how much value exists in a given league-season. Then it divides that value among positions according to fixed shares, and finally among individual players based on what they did.

That accounting constraint is central to GAR. Add up the players on a team, and their value always comes back to what that team actually accomplished.1

How much value is there to give out?

GAR starts with replacement level, defined here as a team that gets outscored by 1.5 goals per game.

That one assumption determines the size of the entire leaguewide pool. Because total goals scored and goals allowed are necessarily equal across a league, total GAR is simply 1.5 goals for every team-game played:

league total GAR = (league GF − league GA) + 1.5 × games
                 = 1.5 × games          // GF = GA leaguewide

team target      = (team GF − team GA) + 1.5 × team GP
                 = goal differential + 1.5 × GP

The second equation is the one GAR has to satisfy for every team. Add up every player on the 2025-26 Panthers, for example, and the result is Florida’s goal differential plus 1.5 goals for every game it played. Not close to that number. Exactly that number.

The same identity holds across all 108 seasons in the database.2

Who gets what share?

Once we know how much GAR exists, we have to decide where it goes.

The leaguewide pool is divided into five buckets, using shares designed to roughly reflect how NHL teams allocate salary: about 60 percent to forwards, 30 percent to defensemen and 10 percent to goaltenders.

Offense — 50%

  • Forwards’ offense — 40%

  • Defensemen’s offense — 10%

Defense and goaltending — 50%

  • Forwards’ defense — 20%

  • Defensemen’s defense — 20%

  • Goaltending — 10%

Those shares are fixed. They don’t change because one season happens to feature unusually good goaltending, unusually weak forward play or a historically great group of defensemen.

Instead, performance determines how the value within each bucket gets distributed. No matter what the statistics say, forwards as a group will receive 40 percent of GAR for offense and 20 percent for defense, defensemen will receive 10 and 20 percent, respectively, and goalies will receive 10 percent.

Offense: Goals Created

Offensive value begins with Goals Created, Justin Kubatko’s stat for dividing a team’s scoring among its skaters according to goals and assists:

GC = (G + 0.5 × A) × team goals / (team goals + 0.5 × team assists)

The useful property here is that every team’s Goals Created totals exactly match its actual goals scored.

GAR then subtracts a replacement-level baseline based on playing time. But instead of choosing that baseline arbitrarily, the model solves for the rate that makes forwards as a group finish with exactly 40 percent of league GAR, and defensemen with exactly 10 percent.

replacement rate = (Σ GC − share × league GAR) / Σ playing time
                   // solved separately for F and D, every season

OGAR = GC − replacement rate × playing time

So the replacement baseline can change from season to season. What doesn’t change is the amount of offensive value available to each position.

Goaltending: Goals Saved Above Average, plus a cushion

Goalies start with Goals Saved Above Average, or GSAA: the difference between how many goals an average goalie would have allowed on the same workload and how many this goalie actually allowed.

From 1955-56 forward, when shot totals are available, “average” means the league save percentage applied to his shots faced. Before that, it means the league’s goals-allowed rate applied to his minutes.

expected GA = shots against × (1 − league SV%)     // 1956–
            = minutes × league GA per minute       // pre-1956

GSAA = expected GA − actual GA

There is one complication. GSAA is measured relative to average, so leaguewide goalie GSAA sits around zero. GAR, meanwhile, needs goaltenders to collectively receive 10 percent of league value.

The difference is filled by a replacement-level cushion, distributed according to workload:

cushion = 0.10 × league GAR − Σ GSAA
GGAR    = GSAA + cushion × (shots faced / league shots faced)

This is probably the most important modeling choice in GAR. The metric takes a goalie’s observed performance at face value. There is no regression toward the mean and no attempt to shrink extreme save percentages.

As a result, goalies occupy both ends of the GAR leaderboard much more often than they would in a more predictive metric. A great goalie season can easily be the most valuable season in the NHL; a terrible one can be the least valuable. Bill Durnan’s 1943-44 season, for instance, produces the highest raw GAR total on record at 87.5 goals.

That is not the only reasonable way to value goaltending. Save percentage is noisy, especially over smaller samples. But GAR is trying to describe what happened, not estimate how likely the performance was to happen again. Under that philosophy, the saves still count.

Skater defense: ice time first, plus-minus second

Defense is where the historical box score gives us the least to work with.

So GAR doesn’t pretend to know more than it does. Most skater defensive value comes from playing time. Each player receives a baseline share according to how much he was on the ice, with defensemen’s minutes weighted twice as heavily so that defensemen and forwards each receive half of the skater-defense pool.

The individual adjustment comes from relative plus-minus: a player’s plus-minus (I know, I know)3 compared with what his own team’s players at the same position would have been expected to produce over the same amount of playing time.

That matters because a forward on a terrible defensive team shouldn’t automatically rate as a terrible defensive player. He’s being compared first with the environment he actually played in.

relative +/− = player +/− − (ice time × team position +/− rate)

adjustment   = (1/7) × position weight × relative +/−
               // position weight: 10/7 for D, 5/7 for F

Forwards and defensemen are then rescaled separately until each group lands on its allotted 20 percent of league GAR.

The result is deliberately restrained. Defensive GAR varies much less than offensive or goaltending GAR, because the historical data simply doesn’t justify pretending we can distinguish skater defense with that level of precision.

Making the books balance!

Getting the leaguewide totals right is only half the job. GAR also has to work team by team.

After the five leaguewide buckets have been distributed, each roster’s total is compared with its target:

team goal differential + 1.5 × games played

Any remaining difference is then redistributed among that team’s players according to playing time, while staying on the appropriate side of the puck. Offensive residuals are assigned through offensive minutes; defensive residuals through defensive minutes.

This final reconciliation is what makes GAR more than a collection of rate stats. If a team outscored its opponents by 50 goals, its players have to account for that somewhere. If it was outscored by 50, they have to account for that too.

Playing time, era-by-era

Obviously, the NHL hasn’t tracked the same statistics for 108 years. GAR uses the best workload measure available in each era.

For skaters, that’s time on ice beginning in 1998-99 and games played before that.

For goalies, it’s shots faced beginning in 1955-56 and minutes played before that.

The units never mix within a season. And because replacement rates are solved independently for each year, switching from games played to time on ice doesn’t mechanically create a jump in player value between 1998 and 1999. Each season is calibrated to itself.

Adjusted GAR

Raw GAR is measured in the goals of its own era. That creates an obvious comparison problem: A goal in 1918 existed in a very different scoring and schedule environment from a goal in 2026.

Adjusted GAR handles this by translating each season onto Hockey-Reference’s neutral statistical environment before applying the same GAR methodology.

That baseline is:

  • an 82-game schedule

  • an 18-skater roster

  • 6.00 combined goals per game

  • 1.67 assists per goal

  • a 3.00 goals-against average

The farther a season is from the modern NHL environment, the more adjustment matters.

Joe Malone’s 44 goals in 20 games in 1917-18 produce 28.5 raw GAR but 79.3 adjusted GAR. Clint Benedict’s 1919-20 season jumps from 45.7 to 95.3.

Modern seasons barely change. Connor McDavid’s 2025-26 total moves by less than one goal.

What it says

Because GAR takes save percentage literally and gives scorers credit for creating goals, the all-time lists wind up dominated by two groups: great goaltenders and Wayne Gretzky.

That is more feature than bug.

What GAR is and isn’t good for

GAR is best used to explain what already happened.

It is intentionally descriptive and backward-looking. The fixed value pool and team-level reconciliation make it especially useful for accounting for the goals a team actually scored and allowed. And the adjusted version gives us a way to compare players who competed in wildly different NHL environments.

What GAR is not designed to do is predict the future.

If a player benefited from shooting luck, GAR counts those goals. If a goalie rode an unsustainably high save percentage for five months, GAR counts those saves. The metric tracks the season it is describing extremely well and the following season much less well.

That’s what we’d expect. A forecasting system should care heavily about which parts of performance persist. GAR mostly doesn’t.

There are two other limitations worth keeping in mind.

First, GAR has no explicit concept of coaching, tactics, system or chemistry. Like any additive player-value statistic, it assumes individual contributions can be separated and added back together.

Second, skater defense is built on plus-minus because, for much of NHL history, that’s essentially all the box score gives us. Defensive GAR is therefore better understood as a conservative allocation of team defensive value than as a precise measurement of individual defensive talent.

Version History:

Sept. 2026 — Rebuilt end-to-end in R. The metric itself is unchanged — same positional shares, replacement level and formulas — but the old Excel and VBA workbooks have been retired. Every season now regenerates directly from scraped source data, with the team-level identity checked automatically on every run.

Sept. 2026 — Elo ratings and playoff odds split into a separate pipeline and are no longer included in this dataset.

Apr. 2026 — Final release of the spreadsheet-era historical file.

Built from Hockey-Reference.com game logs and player statistics. Player values regenerate from source data on each run; the team-level identity — every roster summing to goal differential plus 1.5 goals per game — is checked automatically every time the data set is rebuilt.

1

GAR has two intellectual ancestors, though it isn’t a variant of either one. The idea that player values should reconcile to what a team actually accomplished comes from Point Shares, whose player totals sum to a team's standings points. Measuring value in goals above a replacement-level floor instead comes from Tom Awad’s Goals Versus Threshold — now long gone from the public web, but probably GAR’s closest spiritual predecessor. The main departure here is the fixed positional allocation. In both of those systems, the split of value among positions emerges from the calculations; in GAR, that split is imposed beforehand.

2

There is one source-data exception. In 2006-07, Hockey-Reference’s league goals scored and goals allowed differ by two, leaving the season’s GAR pool off by one goal.

3

There may not be a more maligned stat in hockey than plus-minus… but as Tom Tango has argued before, there is more signal there than it’s often given credit for — it literally represents how well the team did at (basically) even-strength when a player is on the ice! Yes, it takes large samples to tease out a player’s full effect, but it’s weird that plus-minus gets so much hate for its limitations. Nobody is saying it should be the be-all, end-all, yet people pre-emptively criticize that nonexistent strawman to dismiss the stat entirely. It’s bizarre.
